title: [RFC] Interpretation Portal Audio Streaming Architecture and Implementation Roadmap
body:
# Eventyay Interpretation Portal — Audio Streaming Plan

> **Scope:** End-to-end design from mic capture to audience consumption, from local dev to single Docker Compose production deployment.

> **Platform independence:** The interpretation portal is a self-contained product. Its primary output is a set of plain **HLS stream URLs** — one per language per event. These URLs can be consumed by Eventyay (Phase 5), embedded in any third-party event platform, pasted into a player widget, or played directly in a browser. Eventyay integration is optional and additive; it does not affect how the portal operates.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [What We Currently Have](#1-what-we-currently-have)
2. [Gap Analysis — What Is Missing or Broken](#2-gap-analysis)
3. [Architecture and Technology Decisions](#3-architecture-and-technology-decisions)
4. [Phase 1 — Local Media Pipeline + Interpreter Controls](#4-phase-1)
5. [Phase 2 — Multi-Booth and Multi-Event Architecture](#5-phase-2)
6. [Phase 3 — Authentication, RBAC, and Admin Panel](#6-phase-3)
7. [Phase 4 — Interpreter Console UX (Google Meet-style)](#7-phase-4)
8. [Phase 5 — Eventyay Integration (Audio Links)](#8-phase-5)
9. [Phase 6 — Docker Compose Deployment](#9-phase-6)
10. [Full System Architecture (Final State)](#10-full-system-architecture)
11. [Open Questions and Deferred Decisions](#11-open-questions)

---

## 1. What We Currently Have

### 1.1 Interpretation Portal Repository (`eventyay-interpretation-portal/`)

The portal is a **separate, standalone** application from the main Eventyay platform. It consists of two layers:

#### Backend (Python/Flask)

| File | What it does | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `app.py` | Flask 3 + Flask-SocketIO 5 server. Routes for booth state API and Socket.IO realtime coordination (participant management, chat, role assignment, relay handoff). | Working |
| `portal/booth_state.py` | In-memory `BoothRegistry` with thread-safe `RLock`. Manages participants, roles (Active/Backup/Coordinator/Listener), chat, active-interpreter enforcement, and handoff state. | Working |
| `portal/ingest.py` | Legacy `aiortc` WebRTC peer connection handler. **Will be removed** — media ingest is handled by MediaMTX from Phase 1 onward. This file exists from a prior prototype that routed WebRTC through Flask; it is not part of the production architecture. | Deprecated — to be removed |
| `portal/config.py` | Typed `Settings` dataclass from env vars. | Working |

**Flask's role in the production architecture:** Flask handles **coordination only** — booth state, participant management, active interpreter assignment, relay handoff, chat, authentication, RBAC, and the admin panel. Flask does **not** participate in SDP negotiation, RTP processing, media track handling, or HLS generation. All media flows directly from the interpreter's browser to MediaMTX via WHIP.

#### Frontend Stack: Active UI vs. Prototype SPA

The portal has two frontends in the repository, but only one is the **active production path**:

| Path | Stack | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `templates/` + `static/js/` | Jinja2 + vanilla ES modules, Socket.IO | **Active — all new work goes here** |
| `src/` | Vue 3 SPA (Vite build) | Prototype only — not wired to Flask, not used in production |

All further UI development uses **server-rendered Jinja2 templates and plain ES module JavaScript** — no build step, no bundler, no frontend framework. This keeps the portal deployable as a single Python process without a Node.js build stage.

**Why vanilla JS?** The interpreter console is a single-page tool with a fixed set of controls. A framework would add build complexity and bundle size with no meaningful benefit at this scope. Native browser APIs (`RTCPeerConnection`, `getUserMedia`, `MediaDevices`, `AnalyserNode`, `WebSocket`) cover every requirement directly.

The `src/` Vue SPA was an early prototype. It is **not connected** to the Flask backend and will be removed in a dedicated cleanup PR (tracked separately). The `package.json`, `vite.config.js`, and related node config files remain in-tree until that PR lands — do not treat them as the active frontend stack.

#### HLS Output Evidence (Legacy)

`hls-output/` is gitignored (local runtime output, not committed). The legacy `aiortc` ingest pipeline wrote HLS segments here during prototype testing. This directory confirmed that the general concept (browser mic → WebRTC → HLS) works, but the pipeline that generated it (`portal/ingest.py` + `aiortc.MediaRecorder`) is being replaced by MediaMTX from Phase 1. In the production architecture, HLS output is generated and served by MediaMTX — not written to the Flask server's filesystem.

---

### 1.2 Eventyay Main Platform — Stream URL Model

The main platform (`app/eventyay/`) already has infrastructure for per-room stream URLs:

| Model/Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `base/models/stream_schedule.py` — `StreamSchedule` | Room-scoped, time-bound stream URL with `stream_type` choices: `youtube`, `vimeo`, `hls`, `iframe`, `native`. Has a free-form `config` JSONField labelled "language settings". |
| `base/models/schedule.py` — schedule data builder | Injects `stream_url` + `stream_type` into talk-level schedule JSON when a `StreamSchedule` overlaps the talk's time window. |
| `api/views/stream_schedule.py` + `room.py` | REST CRUD for `StreamSchedule`. `/rooms/<pk>/streams/current` returns the active stream for real-time updates. |
| `base/services/room.py` periodic task | Polls for active `StreamSchedule` per room and broadcasts changes over Django Channels (`stream.change` message). Enables live URL switching without page reload. |

**Key insight:** `StreamSchedule.stream_type = 'hls'` and `StreamSchedule.url` already exist as first-class fields. There is no special-purpose interpretation-language field yet, but the `config` JSONField is the designated extension point.

---

## 2. Gap Analysis

### 2.1 What Is Not Working Yet

| Gap | Impact | Root cause |
|---|---|---|
| **No production media server** | Audio ingest relies on `aiortc` (research-grade Python WebRTC) inside Flask — fragile, no STUN/TURN, fails behind NAT | MediaMTX not yet integrated; prototype used aiortc as a stopgap |
| **No authentication or RBAC** | Any person with the URL can join any booth in any role | There is only a flat `BOOTH_ACCESS_TOKEN` shared secret. No per-user identity, no role enforcement beyond the in-memory state machine. |
| **No admin panel** | Booths and events cannot be configured without directly editing env vars or the API | No UI for Admin → Events → Rooms → Booths hierarchy |
| **No interpreter invite links** | Interpreters have no secure, role-scoped URL to access their booth | Token system does not exist yet |
| **No audio device selection** | Interpreter cannot choose which microphone to use | `getUserMedia` uses the browser default device with no UI to change it |
| **In-memory state lost on restart** | All booth state, active interpreters, and sessions vanish on every deploy | No Redis or database persistence layer |
| **Single active ingest per channel not enforced at network level** | Two interpreters could theoretically both WHIP-publish to the same channel if state drifts | Enforcement is purely in-memory in `booth_state.py`; MediaMTX single-publisher mode will add a second layer |
| **No event-level scoping** | Booth IDs are flat strings. No concept of which event or room a booth belongs to | `booth_id` is unstructured. No foreign key to Eventyay data. |
| **No Eventyay integration hook** | The HLS URL produced has no way to appear in Eventyay's `StreamSchedule` for the correct room/language | API bridge does not exist yet |

### 2.2 What Is Working Well (Keep and Build On)

- The **booth state machine** (`booth_state.py`) correctly models roles, active-interpreter enforcement, and handoff.
- The **Socket.IO coordination layer** in `app.py` is functional for participant management, chat, and role events.
- The **browser-side WebRTC offer creation** in `interpreter-booth.js` is solid — it will be retargeted from the custom Flask SDP endpoint to the MediaMTX WHIP endpoint with minimal change.
- The **multi-booth data model** is already designed — each `channel_id` maps to an independent stream.
- Eventyay's `StreamSchedule` model already has `stream_type='hls'` support.

---

## 3. Architecture and Technology Decisions

### 3.1 Core Media Pipeline

The production architecture separates **media transport** (audio ingest + HLS delivery) from **coordination** (booth state, roles, chat, auth):

```
Interpreter Browser
  → WebRTC via WHIP
  → MediaMTX
  → HLS

Flask + Socket.IO (coordination only)
  → booth state management
  → participant coordination
  → active interpreter assignment
  → relay handoff
  → chat
  → authentication + RBAC
  → admin panel
  → Eventyay integration (optional)
```

Flask does **not** participate in SDP negotiation, RTP processing, media track handling, or HLS generation. The browser talks directly to MediaMTX for all audio transport.

### 3.2 Audio Server: MediaMTX

[MediaMTX](https://github.com/bluenviron/mediamtx) is a production-ready, open-source Go-based media server. It is the single component responsible for all audio transport:

| Capability | How MediaMTX handles it |
|---|---|
| **WebRTC ingest** | Accepts WHIP (WebRTC-HTTP Ingest Protocol) — the browser POSTs an SDP offer, MediaMTX returns an SDP answer, then receives Opus audio over RTP/UDP |
| **SDP negotiation** | Handled internally — no application code required |
| **ICE candidate exchange** | Handled internally — MediaMTX manages ICE gathering and connectivity checks |
| **STUN/TURN** | Built-in TURN server (no external `coturn` service needed). Configurable STUN servers for ICE candidates |
| **RTP transport** | Receives Opus RTP from the browser, demuxes, and routes to output |
| **HLS generation** | Transcodes Opus → AAC and segments into a live HLS playlist (`index.m3u8` + `.ts` segments) with configurable segment duration and playlist depth |
| **Single publisher enforcement** | Each path allows only one active WHIP publisher at a time — MediaMTX rejects a second publisher on the same path |

**Why MediaMTX over alternatives:**

| Alternative | Why not |
|---|---|
| **aiortc (Python WebRTC)** | Research-grade library. Fragile ICE handling, no built-in TURN, requires manual FFmpeg process for HLS, runs inside Flask's Python process creating threading and stability issues. Not suitable for production. |
| **Livekit** | Full WebRTC SFU with mixing, recording, egress. Powerful but significantly more complex to operate and overkill for single-stream-per-booth audio ingest. |
| **Janus** | Mature WebRTC gateway but requires extensive plugin configuration and C-level operations. More operational overhead than MediaMTX for this use case. |
| **Custom coturn + FFmpeg** | Requires assembling multiple services (TURN server + SDP signalling + RTP receiver + FFmpeg transcoder + HLS segmenter). MediaMTX does all of this in one 20MB binary. |

MediaMTX runs as a single stateless Docker container (~20MB image). Each stream is identified by a **path** (e.g., `pycon-2026/en`). When a browser publishes to a path via WHIP, MediaMTX immediately begins generating an HLS playlist at that path's URL.

### 3.3 Transport Protocol: WHIP

**What it is:** WHIP (WebRTC-HTTP Ingest Protocol) is an IETF-standardised way for a browser to push a WebRTC audio/video stream to a media server using a single HTTP POST. The browser sends an SDP offer as the request body; the server responds with an SDP answer; then RTP/UDP flows directly browser → server.

**How it works under the hood (educational — these steps are handled by MediaMTX, not by our code):**

1. Browser calls `navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true })` to capture the mic
2. Browser creates an `RTCPeerConnection`, adds the audio track, calls `createOffer()`
3. Browser POSTs the SDP offer to `https://media-server/whip/{path}` with `Content-Type: application/sdp`
4. MediaMTX parses the offer, generates ICE candidates (using its built-in STUN/TURN), creates an SDP answer
5. MediaMTX returns the SDP answer as the HTTP response body (status 201)
6. Browser calls `setRemoteDescription(answer)` — the WebRTC connection is established
7. Opus audio frames flow via RTP/RTCP from the browser to MediaMTX over UDP (or TCP/TURN if UDP is blocked)
8. MediaMTX transcodes Opus → AAC and writes HLS segments to its internal origin server

**What our code does:** Steps 1–3 and 6. Everything else is MediaMTX's responsibility.

**Why WHIP over a custom SDP endpoint:** The existing `POST /api/interpreter/connect` in Flask was effectively a hand-rolled version of this protocol, except it also ran aiortc to terminate the WebRTC connection inside the Python process. WHIP removes Flask from the media path entirely, uses an IETF standard, and means any WHIP-compatible media server can be swapped in later without changing browser code.

### 3.4 HLS Delivery

**What HLS is:** HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) is Apple's adaptive streaming protocol. A server writes a rolling playlist file (`index.m3u8`) listing short audio/video segment files (`.ts`). A player fetches the playlist periodically and downloads new segments as they appear — this is how live streaming works on the web without any persistent connection.

**Why HLS over WebRTC for audience delivery:** WebRTC gives < 500ms latency but requires a persistent signalling server per viewer and does not scale cost-effectively to hundreds of simultaneous listeners. HLS scales horizontally to any number of viewers via a standard CDN, works in every browser natively on Safari and with `hls.js` everywhere else, and the 2–4s latency is acceptable for simultaneous interpretation.

**Why not DASH or other formats:** HLS has universal browser support and MediaMTX outputs it natively. DASH is equally capable but requires additional player library support with no advantage at this scale.

MediaMTX serves HLS at `http://media-server:8888/<path>/index.m3u8`. An Nginx reverse proxy sits in front to apply CORS headers (so any origin — Eventyay, a third-party embed, or a standalone player — can fetch the playlist) and to terminate TLS. The public-facing URL is what operators share and what any consumer (Eventyay or otherwise) plugs in.

### 3.5 State Persistence

**Why Redis for Socket.IO:** Flask-SocketIO in multi-worker mode requires a message queue so that an event emitted by worker A reaches clients connected to worker B. Redis pub/sub is the standard Flask-SocketIO backend for this. Without it, Socket.IO events only reach clients connected to the same process.

**Why SQLite for booth/auth data (Phase 3):** The portal's relational data (events, rooms, booths, invite tokens) has a simple schema with low write volume. SQLite handles this without an additional service. PostgreSQL can be substituted by changing one env var (`DATABASE_URL`) if the deployment grows.

The PostgreSQL database of the main Eventyay platform is **not** touched by the portal. The portal only calls Eventyay's REST API when Eventyay integration is enabled — and that is entirely optional.

### 3.6 Why Flask

Flask is kept for the coordination layer because:
- It already integrates with the working booth state machine (`booth_state.py`)
- Flask-SocketIO provides the realtime coordination layer (booth state sync, chat, role events) with minimal ceremony
- Jinja2 template rendering is native to Flask — no template engine to add
- The portal is a small, single-purpose service; Django or FastAPI would be overengineered

**Flask's boundary is clear:** it handles everything *except* audio transport. It never touches SDP, RTP, media tracks, or HLS segments. The browser communicates with Flask for coordination (Socket.IO) and with MediaMTX for audio (WHIP).

### 3.7 Why Nginx

Nginx sits in front of both Flask (portal) and MediaMTX (media) to:
1. Terminate TLS so both services serve `https://`
2. Set CORS response headers on HLS responses — MediaMTX does not set them by default
3. Enforce `Cache-Control: no-cache` on HLS playlists (critical for live streams)
4. Proxy WebSocket upgrades for Socket.IO
5. Provide a single public IP/hostname for the entire stack

---

## 4. Phase 1 — Local Media Pipeline + Interpreter Controls

**Goal:** An interpreter opens the portal, joins a booth, clicks "Go Live", and audio flows directly from their browser to MediaMTX via WHIP. An HLS stream appears at a local URL. All mic controls (device selection, level meter, mute/unmute) work.

### 4.1 Steps

#### Step 1 — Run MediaMTX Locally via Docker

Start MediaMTX as a Docker container alongside the Flask portal:

```bash
# Pull and run MediaMTX
docker run --rm -d --name mediamtx \
  -p 8888:8888 \
  -p 8889:8889 \
  bluenviron/mediamtx:latest
```

This gives two endpoints out of the box:
- **WHIP ingest:** `http://localhost:8889/whip/{path}` — where the browser sends audio
- **HLS output:** `http://localhost:8888/{path}/index.m3u8` — where the audience fetches audio

No configuration file is needed for the default setup. MediaMTX auto-creates paths on first publish.

#### Step 2 — Configure MediaMTX (`mediamtx.yml`)

For local development, create a minimal `mediamtx.yml`:

```yaml
# mediamtx.yml — local dev configuration
logLevel: info
logDestinations: [stdout]

# WHIP ingest
webrtcAddress: :8889
webrtcEncryption: no

# HLS output
hlsAddress: :8888
hlsEncryption: no
hlsAlwaysRemux: yes
hlsSegmentDuration: 2s
hlsSegmentMaxSize: 50MB

# All paths auto-created, single publisher per path
pathDefaults:
  record: no
```

Mount it:
```bash
docker run --rm -d --name mediamtx \
  -v $(pwd)/mediamtx.yml:/mediamtx.yml:ro \
  -p 8888:8888 -p 8889:8889 \
  bluenviron/mediamtx:latest
```

**What MediaMTX handles internally at this point:** When a browser POSTs a WHIP offer to `http://localhost:8889/whip/test-booth`, MediaMTX:
1. Parses the SDP offer
2. Generates ICE candidates (localhost only — no STUN/TURN needed for local dev)
3. Creates and returns an SDP answer
4. Accepts the incoming Opus RTP stream
5. Transcodes Opus → AAC
6. Writes a live HLS playlist at `http://localhost:8888/test-booth/index.m3u8`

None of this requires any Flask code, aiortc, FFmpeg processes, or custom SDP endpoints.

#### Step 3 — Browser WHIP Integration

Update `interpreter-booth.js` to POST the SDP offer directly to MediaMTX's WHIP endpoint instead of the legacy Flask `/api/interpreter/connect` route:

```js
// static/js/interpreter-booth.js — Go Live flow

async function startLiveIngest() {
  // 1. Acquire mic stream with selected device
  const stream = await ensureMicStream();

  // 2. Create RTCPeerConnection (no ICE servers needed for local dev;
  //    STUN/TURN is configured in MediaMTX for production)
  const pc = new RTCPeerConnection();
  stream.getAudioTracks().forEach(track => pc.addTrack(track, stream));

  // 3. Create SDP offer
  const offer = await pc.createOffer({ offerToReceiveAudio: false });
  await pc.setLocalDescription(offer);

  // 4. POST the SDP offer to MediaMTX WHIP endpoint
  const whipUrl = `${MEDIAMTX_WHIP_URL}/${channelId}`;
  const res = await fetch(whipUrl, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/sdp' },
    body: pc.localDescription.sdp,
  });

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`WHIP failed: ${res.status}`);

  // 5. Set the SDP answer from MediaMTX
  const answerSdp = await res.text();
  await pc.setRemoteDescription({ type: 'answer', sdp: answerSdp });

  // 6. Notify Flask that ingest is active (coordination only)
  socket.emit('booth:update-state', {
    mic_active: true,
    ingest_connected: true,
  });

  state.peerConnection = pc;
}
```

**Key point:** Flask never sees the SDP offer or answer. The browser talks directly to MediaMTX for the media path. Flask is only notified via Socket.IO that the interpreter has gone live (for booth state tracking).

#### Step 4 — Audio Device Selection

Interpreters must be able to select which audio input device to use (headset mic, USB audio interface, etc.). Add device enumeration and a `<select>` dropdown to the booth page:

```js
// static/js/interpreter-booth.js — device enumeration
async function populateMicDevices() {
  // Must call getUserMedia first to get permission before enumerateDevices labels appear
  const tempStream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true });
  tempStream.getTracks().forEach(t => t.stop());

  const devices = await navigator.mediaDevices.enumerateDevices();
  const audioInputs = devices.filter(d => d.kind === 'audioinput');

  const select = document.getElementById('mic-device-select');
  select.innerHTML = '';
  for (const device of audioInputs) {
    const opt = document.createElement('option');
    opt.value = device.deviceId;
    opt.textContent = device.label || `Microphone ${select.options.length + 1}`;
    select.appendChild(opt);
  }
}

// Re-populate when devices change (plug/unplug)
navigator.mediaDevices.addEventListener('devicechange', populateMicDevices);

// When starting ingest, use the selected device
async function ensureMicStream() {
  const deviceId = document.getElementById('mic-device-select').value;
  state.micStream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({
    audio: {
      deviceId: deviceId ? { exact: deviceId } : undefined,
      echoCancellation: true,
      noiseSuppression: true,
      autoGainControl: true,
    }
  });
  return state.micStream;
}
```

Also add a **mic level meter** (AnalyserNode → canvas bar) so the interpreter can confirm the selected device is picking up audio before going live:

```js
function startMicMeter(stream) {
  const ctx = new AudioContext();
  const source = ctx.createMediaStreamSource(stream);
  const analyser = ctx.createAnalyser();
  analyser.fftSize = 256;
  source.connect(analyser);

  const data = new Uint8Array(analyser.frequencyBinCount);
  const canvas = document.getElementById('mic-meter');
  const canvasCtx = canvas.getContext('2d');

  function draw() {
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
    analyser.getByteFrequencyData(data);
    const volume = data.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / data.length;
    canvasCtx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
    canvasCtx.fillStyle = volume > 10 ? '#22c55e' : '#374151';
    canvasCtx.fillRect(0, 0, (volume / 128) * canvas.width, canvas.height);
  }
  draw();
}
```

#### Step 5 — Mute / Unmute

Mute toggles `track.enabled` on the active mic stream. The WebRTC connection stays alive — the stream continues with silence at the source:

```js
function toggleMicMute() {
  if (!state.micStream) return;
  const track = state.micStream.getAudioTracks()[0];
  track.enabled = !track.enabled;
  state.micMuted = !track.enabled;
  // Update UI indicator
  updateMuteButton(state.micMuted);
}
```

#### Step 6 — Preflight Checklist

Before showing "Go Live", run automated checks. Build in `templates/` + `static/js/` (the prototype Vue `PreflightChecklist.vue` can be used as a logic reference, but the implementation is plain JS + Jinja2):

```js
async function runPreflightChecks() {
  const checks = {};

  // 1. Mic permission
  try {
    const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true });
    stream.getTracks().forEach(t => t.stop());
    checks.micPermission = { ok: true, label: 'Microphone permission granted' };
  } catch {
    checks.micPermission = { ok: false, label: 'Microphone permission denied' };
  }

  // 2. Audio device detected
  const devices = await navigator.mediaDevices.enumerateDevices();
  const audioInputs = devices.filter(d => d.kind === 'audioinput');
  checks.audioDevice = audioInputs.length > 0
    ? { ok: true, label: `Audio device detected: ${audioInputs[0].label}` }
    : { ok: false, label: 'No audio input device found' };

  // 3. MediaMTX reachable
  try {
    const res = await fetch(MEDIAMTX_HLS_BASE, { method: 'GET', mode: 'no-cors' });
    checks.mediaServer = { ok: true, label: 'Media server reachable' };
  } catch {
    checks.mediaServer = { ok: false, label: 'Media server unreachable' };
  }

  return checks;
}
```

#### Step 7 — HLS Playback Validation

After going live, verify the stream is playable. Open the HLS URL in a browser tab or use a simple inline player:

```
http://localhost:8888/{channelId}/index.m3u8
```

For automated validation, add a small test on the booth page:

```js
async function validateHlsOutput(channelId) {
  const url = `${MEDIAMTX_HLS_BASE}/${channelId}/index.m3u8`;
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (res.ok) {
    const text = await res.text();
    return text.includes('#EXTM3U');
  }
  return false;
}
```

#### Step 8 — Remove aiortc from the Critical Path

With MediaMTX handling all media transport, `portal/ingest.py` is no longer used. In Phase 1:

1. Remove the import and initialisation of `IngestService` from `app.py`
2. Remove the `/api/interpreter/connect` and `/api/interpreter/disconnect` routes (the browser no longer calls them)
3. Keep `/api/interpreter/status` if needed for health monitoring, but repoint it at MediaMTX's API
4. Remove `aiortc` and `av` from `pyproject.toml` dependencies
5. Delete `portal/ingest.py`

Flask retains all booth state, participant, and coordination routes. Only the media-handling routes and imports are removed.

### 4.2 End-to-End Local Test Sequence

```
1. docker run mediamtx (:8888 HLS, :8889 WHIP)
2. uv run python app.py (:5000 Flask)
3. Open http://localhost:5000/interpreter/test-booth
4. Select mic device from dropdown
5. Verify level meter responds to voice
6. Click "Go Live"
   → Browser POSTs SDP offer to http://localhost:8889/whip/test-booth
   → MediaMTX returns SDP answer
   → Opus/RTP flows browser → MediaMTX
7. Open http://localhost:8888/test-booth/index.m3u8 in VLC or browser
   → Live audio plays with ~2-4s delay
8. Click "Mute" → audio goes silent in HLS playback
9. Click "Unmute" → audio resumes
10. Click "Stop" → HLS stream ends
```

### 4.3 Phase 1 Success Criteria

- [ ] MediaMTX runs locally via Docker
- [ ] Interpreter clicks "Go Live" and browser streams directly to MediaMTX (not Flask)
- [ ] HLS playlist appears at `http://localhost:8888/{path}/index.m3u8` within 4 seconds
- [ ] Mute/unmute toggles mic track — reflected in HLS playback
- [ ] Mic device dropdown populates with all available audio inputs
- [ ] Selecting a different device and clicking "Go Live" uses that device
- [ ] Mic level meter responds visually to voice input
- [ ] Preflight checklist validates mic permission, device, and server reachability
- [ ] `aiortc` and `av` removed from `pyproject.toml`
- [ ] `portal/ingest.py` deleted
- [ ] Flask `/api/interpreter/connect` and `/api/interpreter/disconnect` routes removed

---

## 5. Phase 2 — Multi-Booth, Multi-Event Data Model

**Goal:** Support `N` booths for `M` events simultaneously, with exactly one active audio stream per language per event.

### 5.1 Booth Identity Schema

A booth is identified by three coordinates:

```
{event_slug} / {language_code} / {booth_instance}
```

Where `booth_instance` exists for redundancy (Primary/Backup). At any time, **only one** booth instance per `{event_slug}/{language_code}` is the active publisher. The others are listening/standby.

MediaMTX path: `{event_slug}/{language_code}` (single active stream per language per event)  
Flask booth ID: `{event_slug}-{language_code}` (e.g. `pycon2026-en`, `pycon2026-es`)

### 5.2 Updated Booth State Model

The existing `BoothRegistry` in `booth_state.py` needs two additions:

```python
@dataclass
class Booth:
    booth_id: str
    language: str
    channel_id: str       # = MediaMTX path (event_slug/language_code)
    event_slug: str       # NEW — links booth to an Eventyay event
    room_id: int | None   # NEW — links to Eventyay Room FK for StreamSchedule update
    ...
```

The `channel_id` is the authoritative MediaMTX path. When the active interpreter goes live, only one `POST /whip/{channel_id}` is valid at a time — MediaMTX enforces single publisher per path by default.

### 5.3 Active-Interpreter Enforcement (Multi-Layer)

```
Layer 1: Flask booth_state.py     — only active interpreter role can set mic_active=True
Layer 2: Flask /api/booth route   — returns the WHIP URL only when caller is active interpreter
Layer 3: MediaMTX                 — rejects second WHIP publisher on same path (single publisher mode)
```

Three independent layers means no race condition can result in two live audio streams for the same language.

### 5.4 Booth Bootstrap Flow

```
1. Eventyay organiser creates a language channel for their event
   → calls Interpretation Portal API: POST /api/events/{event_slug}/booths
   → Portal creates Booth entry, returns booth_id and join URL

2. Interpreter navigates to: https://portal.domain/interpreter/{event_slug}/{language_code}
   → Portal serves the booth page, joined to the correct booth

3. Coordinator assigns active interpreter
   → Socket.IO booth:set-active event

4. Active interpreter clicks "Go Live"
   → Flask validates active role
   → Returns WHIP URL: {mediamtx_url}/whip/{event_slug}/{language_code}
   → Browser streams to MediaMTX

5. HLS becomes available at: {media_url}/{event_slug}/{language_code}/index.m3u8
```

### 5.5 Multi-Event Namespace Isolation

Each event gets its own namespace in MediaMTX paths. There is no cross-event interference. An organiser for `fosdem-2027` cannot see or affect paths for `pycon-2026`.

---

## 6. Phase 3 — Authentication, RBAC, and Admin Panel

**Goal:** Every user has a verified identity and scoped access. Admins configure the hierarchy; interpreters arrive via invite links and can only access their assigned booth.

### 6.1 Role Model

Five roles exist in the portal, each with distinct permissions:

| Role | Who | Can do |
|---|---|---|
| **Super Admin** | Portal operator | Create/delete events; manage all admins; view all booths |
| **Event Admin** | Conference organiser | Create/edit rooms and booths for their event; generate invite links; view all booths in their event |
| **Coordinator** | Booth technical lead | Assign active interpreter; view participant roster; send booth chat; cannot go live |
| **Interpreter** | Human interpreter | Join assigned booth; go live (if active); mute/unmute; pass relay; chat |
| **Listener** | Observer, trainee | Join booth audio-only; chat; cannot go live or assign roles |

Role is embedded in the invite token — not user-selectable at join time.

### 6.2 Database Model

The portal adds a small **SQLite database** (upgradeable to PostgreSQL for scale). Schema:

```
events
  id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY  -- matches Eventyay event_slug
  display_name  TEXT
  created_at    DATETIME
  admin_secret  TEXT              -- hashed, used to generate invite tokens

rooms
  id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY  -- e.g. "main-hall", "room-b"
  event_id      TEXT REFERENCES events(id)
  display_name  TEXT
  eventyay_room_id  INTEGER       -- FK to Eventyay Room, nullable

booths
  id            TEXT PRIMARY KEY  -- e.g. "pycon-2026-en"
  room_id       TEXT REFERENCES rooms(id)
  event_id      TEXT REFERENCES events(id)
  language_code TEXT              -- ISO 639-1, e.g. "en", "es", "fr"
  language_name TEXT              -- "English", "Spanish", "French"
  mediamtx_path TEXT              -- "{event_id}/{language_code}"
  hls_url       TEXT              -- public HLS URL when live, null otherwise
  created_at    DATETIME

invite_tokens
  token         TEXT PRIMARY KEY  -- cryptographically random, 32 bytes, hex
  booth_id      TEXT REFERENCES booths(id)
  role          TEXT              -- coordinator | interpreter | listener
  label         TEXT              -- "John Smith (EN interpreter)"
  expires_at    DATETIME          -- null = never expires
  used_at       DATETIME          -- null = not yet used; single-use optional
  created_by    TEXT              -- admin who issued it
```

SQLAlchemy or plain `sqlite3` with explicit SQL — no ORM framework overhead needed at this scale.

### 6.3 Token-Based Authentication Flow

Invite links encode the token directly in the URL:

```
https://portal.your-domain.com/join/{token}
```

**Flow:**

```
1. Event Admin creates a booth (pycon-2026 / Main Hall / English)
2. Admin generates an invite token for role=interpreter, label="John Smith"
3. Admin copies the invite link and sends it to John
4. John clicks: https://portal.your-domain.com/join/{token}
5. Flask validates token:
   - Not expired
   - Booth exists
   - (Optional: single-use check — mark used_at)
6. Flask issues a signed session cookie:
   { participant_id, booth_id, role, label, event_id }
   Signed with SECRET_KEY (itsdangerous.URLSafeTimedSerializer)
7. John is redirected to: /interpreter/{event_id}/{booth_id}
   The page loads with their role pre-set — no form to fill in
```

The session cookie expires after 24 hours. John can re-use his invite link to refresh (unless single-use mode is enabled).

**No passwords. No registration form. The invite link IS the credential.**

### 6.4 Admin Panel Routes

The admin panel is server-rendered Jinja2 (same as the interpreter console). No separate admin framework — plain Flask routes with a superadmin session guard.

```
GET  /admin/                              → Dashboard: event list + live booth status
GET  /admin/login                         → Superadmin login form (password from env var)
POST /admin/login                         → Sets superadmin session cookie

GET  /admin/events/                       → Event list
POST /admin/events/                       → Create event
GET  /admin/events/{event_id}/            → Event detail: rooms list, booth list, live status
POST /admin/events/{event_id}/delete      → Delete event (confirmation required)

GET  /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/      → Room list for event
POST /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/      → Create room
GET  /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/   → Room detail: booth list
POST /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/delete  → Delete room

GET  /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/booths/        → Booth list
POST /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/booths/        → Create booth (language_code, language_name)
GET  /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/booths/{booth_id}/  → Booth detail:
                                                                      live status,
                                                                      HLS URL (copy button),
                                                                      participant roster,
                                                                      invite token list
POST /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/booths/{booth_id}/tokens/  → Generate invite token
POST /admin/events/{event_id}/rooms/{room_id}/booths/{booth_id}/tokens/{token}/revoke  → Revoke token
```

**Admin Dashboard view example:**

```
Eventyay Interpretation Portal — Admin
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Events (3)                                    [+ New Event]

  PyCon 2026
  ├─ Main Hall
  │   ├─ 🟢 English (pycon-2026/en)  [LIVE]  HLS: https://...  [Copy]
  │   ├─ 🟢 Spanish (pycon-2026/es)  [LIVE]  HLS: https://...  [Copy]
  │   └─ ⚪ French  (pycon-2026/fr)  [OFFLINE]
  └─ Workshop Room B
      └─ ⚪ German  (pycon-2026/de)  [OFFLINE]

  FOSDEM 2027
  └─ Janson Auditorium
      └─ ⚪ French  (fosdem-2027/fr)  [OFFLINE]
```

### 6.5 Generating Invite Links (Admin UI)

On the booth detail page, the admin sees a table of tokens:

```
Invite Tokens for: PyCon 2026 / Main Hall / English
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Label               Role          Expires    Used      Actions
John Smith          interpreter   never      –         [Revoke] [Copy Link]
Maria Garcia        interpreter   never      –         [Revoke] [Copy Link]
Sarah Lee           coordinator   never      –         [Revoke] [Copy Link]
                                                        [+ Generate Token]
```

The "Copy Link" button copies `https://portal.domain/join/{token}` to clipboard. Admin sends it via email/Slack/etc.

### 6.6 RBAC Enforcement in Flask Routes

Every interpreter-facing and admin route is guarded:

```python
# portal/auth.py

from functools import wraps
from flask import session, abort, redirect, url_for

def require_role(*roles):
    """Decorator: ensure current session has one of the given roles."""
    def decorator(f):
        @wraps(f)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            participant = session.get('participant')
            if not participant:
                return redirect(url_for('join_page'))
            if participant['role'] not in roles:
                abort(403)
            # Ensure the participant is accessing their own booth
            booth_id = kwargs.get('booth_id')
            if booth_id and participant['booth_id'] != booth_id:
                abort(403)
            return f(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator

def require_admin(f):
    @wraps(f)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        if not session.get('is_admin'):
            return redirect(url_for('admin_login'))
        return f(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper
```

Usage:

```python
@app.route('/interpreter/<event_id>/<booth_id>')
@require_role('interpreter', 'coordinator', 'listener')
def interpreter_console(event_id, booth_id):
    ...

# Only coordinators and active interpreters can call set-active
@socketio.on('booth:set-active')
def handle_set_active(data):
    participant = session.get('participant')
    if participant['role'] not in ('coordinator', 'interpreter'):
        emit('booth:error', {'message': 'Insufficient role'})
        return
    ...
```

### 6.7 Superadmin Password

The superadmin login uses a bcrypt-hashed password stored in the environment:

```bash
ADMIN_PASSWORD_HASH=<bcrypt hash of your password>
```

There is intentionally **only one** superadmin account. Event admins are managed via the same invite token system (role=`event_admin`, scoped to a specific event).

### 6.8 Phase 3 Success Criteria

- [ ] Admin can log in at `/admin/` with the configured password
- [ ] Admin can create Event → Room → Booth hierarchy via the UI
- [ ] Admin can generate an invite link for coordinator/interpreter/listener roles
- [ ] Clicking an invite link lands the user on the correct booth page with the correct role pre-set
- [ ] An interpreter with a Spanish booth token cannot access the English booth
- [ ] A listener cannot trigger "Go Live" — the button is absent from their UI
- [ ] Expired or revoked tokens return a 403 with a clear message
- [ ] Superadmin can revoke any token from the admin panel

title: Caption overlap in ImageComparePane
body: **Bug Description** Image captions/titles in `ImageComparePane` can visually interfere with image content when comparing images across environments. Depending on image size and layout constraints, captions may become cramped or appear partially overlapped by image content, reducing readability. **Reproduction Steps** 1. Start the Visdom server: 2. Run a script that creates images with matching titles across multiple environments. 3. Open multiple environments simultaneously (`animals` and `metrics`). 4. Observe the generated image comparison pane. **Expected behavior** - Captions/titles should remain clearly visible. - Image content should stay within its allocated bounds. - Captions should have dedicated layout space and should not visually interfere with images. **Actual behavior** - Captions/titles may appear visually cramped or partially overlap with image content. - Image content and labels compete for layout space. **Screenshots**

title: Local development may use installed Visdom package instead of checked-out repository source
body:
## Bug Description

Running Visdom locally using:

```bash
python -m visdom.server
```

may silently import an already installed `visdom` package from `site-packages` instead of the checked-out repository source.

This can cause confusing behavior where frontend changes compile successfully, but the UI still shows old behavior.

---

## Reproduction Steps

1. Clone the repository
2. Modify frontend files and run:

```bash
npm run build
python -m visdom.server
```

3. Observe that local changes may not appear
4. Verify import source:

```bash
python -c "import visdom; print(visdom.__file__)"
```

5. Observe that Visdom is imported from `site-packages` instead of the local repository.

---

## Expected behavior

Local development should use the checked-out repository source or clearly warn when an installed package shadows it.

---

## Additional context

This was resolved locally using:

```bash
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/py:$PYTHONPATH
```

title: OAuth / SSO provider client secrets are stored in plaintext and visible to server admins

labels.name: verified
labels.description: Opened by a member of eventyay-core or eventyay-devs

body: **Describe the bug** OAuth / SSO provider credentials (`client_id` and especially `client_secret`) configured by event organizers are currently stored in plaintext in the database (`socialaccount_socialapp` table). This means developers or administrators with database access on the Eventyay server can directly view third-party OAuth credentials belonging to organizers who configure their own SSO providers (Google, Wikimedia, etc.). In a multi-tenant platform, these credentials belong to the event organizers and should ideally not be readable in plaintext by platform operators. **Expected behavior** Sensitive OAuth credentials should be protected using industry-standard secret management practices. Possible approaches: - Encrypt `client_secret` values at rest using application-level encryption - Store secrets using a dedicated secrets manager / vault solution - Restrict plaintext visibility in admin panels and DB tooling - Support secure key rotation mechanisms The goal is to ensure that even if developers or DB admins have database access, organizer-owned OAuth secrets are not trivially exposed. **Screenshots** Current database view showing plaintext OAuth credentials stored in `socialaccount_socialapp`: **Additional context** Current discussion raised the concern that: - Event organizers may configure their own OAuth apps - Their provider secrets become visible to anyone with DB access - A server compromise or insider access could expose third-party OAuth credentials This appears to be more of a security hardening / secrets-management issue rather than a functional bug, but it impacts tenant isolation and credential security best practices.

title: [Bug] Wrong updates
body:
## Bug Description
The Scrum Report contribution summary shows inconsistent and incomplete data depending on the selected date range. Specifically, when selecting **May 3 to May 4**, multiple contributions (PR reviews, issues) are displayed correctly. However, when extending the range to **May 3 to May 5**, some of these previously visible contributions disappear instead of being cumulatively included.

This creates a data inconsistency where expanding the date range results in **loss of entries**, which breaks expected reporting behavior.

---

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Go to the Contributions / Scrum Report section
2. Select date range:
   - From: **May 3, 2026**
   - To: **May 4, 2026**
3. Observe the list of contributions (multiple PR reviews + issue updates are shown)
4. Change the date range:
   - From: **May 3, 2026**
   - To: **May 5, 2026**
5. Compare the results

---

### Expected Behavior
- Contributions should be **cumulative across the selected date range**
- Expanding the range (May 3 → May 5) should include:
  - All entries from May 3–4
  - Plus any additional entries from May 5
- No previously visible contributions should disappear

---

### Actual Behavior
- When extending the date range from **May 3–4 → May 3–5**:
  - Some contributions (PR reviews, entries) are **missing**
  - The report shows **fewer items instead of more**
- This indicates a possible issue with:
  - Date filtering logic
  - Aggregation / grouping layer
  - OR backend query boundaries

---

### Screenshots
- Case 1 (May 3–4): Shows multiple PR reviews and issue updates  
- Case 2 (May 3–5): Missing several entries from the previous range

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/04312e5d-a6be-48da-b793-11d2afd761fd
  

---

title: [Bug] Incorrect filtering: issues without activity still appear in "Updated Issues"
body: ## Bug Description The Scrum Helper incorrectly includes issues in the "Updated Issues" section even when there has been no activity on those issues during the selected reporting period. For example, issue #1156 appears under "Updated Issues" despite no updates, comments, commits, or status changes within the selected timeframe. --- ### Steps to Reproduce Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. Open Scrum Helper 2. Select a specific reporting period (e.g., last 24 hours / custom date range) 3. Generate the daily report 4. Observe the "Updated Issues" section 5. Notice issues listed where: - The user is the author - BUT there has been **no activity during the selected period** --- ### Expected Behavior Only issues with **actual activity within the selected time window** should appear in the "Updated Issues" section. Valid activity includes: - Comments - Commits / PR references - Status changes (open/close/reopen) - Label or assignment updates Issues merely created or owned by the user should **not** be included unless activity occurred during the period. --- ### Actual Behavior Issues authored by the user are being included in the "Updated Issues" section regardless of whether any activity occurred during the selected timeframe. This leads to: - Misleading daily reports - Inflated activity logs - Reduced trust in generated summaries --- ### Screenshots Example: Issue #1156 is shown as "Updated" despite no activity in the selected period. --- ### Additional Context Likely root cause: - The filtering logic may be based on: - `author == current_user` instead of - `last_activity_timestamp ∈ selected_time_range` Suggested fix direction: - Filter using: - `updated_at` (GitHub issue field) - OR event timeline activity - Ensure strict time-window validation before inclusion Impact: - Medium severity (report accuracy issue) - Affects productivity tracking and standup reporting quality --- ## Contribution Checklist - [x] I have searched existing issues to ensure this bug hasn't been reported - [x] I have provided clear reproduction steps - [x] I have included relevant environment details - [x] I have described both expected and actual behavior

title: OAuth (Wikimedia) login fails for existing email account; redirects to password login instead
body: ## Title OAuth (Wikimedia) login fails for existing email account; redirects to password login instead --- ## Describe the bug Previously, users could log in using Wikimedia OAuth even if an account already existed with the same email (used for email/password login). Now, when attempting to log in via Wikimedia (with the same email as an existing account), the system does not authenticate via OAuth. Instead, it sends an email stating that an account already exists and instructs the user to log in using email/password. This creates a broken authentication flow where: - Same email exists across both login methods - OAuth login is not linked or recognized - User is blocked from using Wikimedia login --- ## Steps to reproduce 1. Create or have an existing account using email/password 2. Ensure the same email is associated with a Wikimedia account 3. Attempt to log in via Wikimedia OAuth 4. Observe the response/email --- ## Expected behavior - Wikimedia OAuth login should authenticate successfully if the email matches an existing account - OR the system should automatically link the Wikimedia account to the existing user - Users should be able to log in via either method seamlessly (email/password OR Wikimedia) --- ## Actual behavior - OAuth login fails - User receives an email stating "Account Already Exists" - System forces login via email/password instead of allowing Wikimedia login --- ## Screenshots

title: General Settings save fails because shared form requires fields not present on that page
body: ## Title General Settings save fails because shared form requires fields not present on that page ## Summary Saving changes in Control → Event → General Settings can fail with a generic settings validation error, even when editing unrelated fields such as currency, dates, or basic options. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open Control Panel for an event. 2. Go to Event Settings → General. 3. Change any basic field (for example currency or timeline field). 4. Click Save. 5. Observe validation failure. ## Actual Behavior Form submission fails with a generic settings validation error. ## Expected Behavior General Settings should save successfully when submitted fields are valid. ## Root Cause The page uses a shared form class that includes required fields for attendee name scheme configuration. Those fields are not rendered/submitted on General Settings, but were still treated as required during form validation. As a result, bound form validation fails even for unrelated changes.

title: Control event settings can fail with "Settings form validation failed" when optional order modification deadline inputs are omitted
body: ## Title Control event settings can fail with "Settings form validation failed" when optional order modification deadline inputs are omitted ## Description Saving General Settings in the organizer control panel can fail even when the Last date of modifications value is effectively "Not set". This happens when the multi-part relative date inputs are missing or partially missing in the submitted form payload. The form then fails validation with a generic error banner: - Settings form validation failed. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Open an event in Control Panel. 2. Navigate to Settings → General. 3. In Order Modification, keep or set last modification date as Not set. 4. Submit the settings form from a state where the relative date sub-inputs are not present in POST (for example after dependency-driven UI toggling or partial payload submission). 5. Observe validation failure. ## Actual Behavior Form submission fails with a settings validation error even though no deadline should be required. ## Expected Behavior If the deadline field is optional and its sub-inputs are missing, backend should treat it as Not set and save should succeed. ## Impact - Organizers see blocking validation failure on legitimate settings submissions. - Creates confusion because UI may not clearly show a field-level issue. - Can prevent updating unrelated settings. ## Root Cause Relative date multi-value form fields assumed status sub-inputs were always present. When omitted, validation logic did not normalize missing optional payloads to unset.

## Describe the enhancement

The search feature on `dev.eventyay.com` currently lacks a standard keyboard shortcut for quick access.

Modern web platforms commonly support a global search shortcut:

- **Ctrl + K** (Windows/Linux)
- **Cmd + K** (macOS)

Adding this will improve accessibility, usability, and align Eventyay with industry-standard UX patterns.

---

- Pressing **Ctrl + K** or **Cmd + K** from anywhere on the start page should:
  - Automatically focus the search input field
  - Allow users to immediately start typing their query

---

This shortcut is widely adopted across major platforms like Discord, Notion, Slack, etc and users increasingly expect it as a default productivity feature.

---

This issue is separate from the main bug where the search box is non-functional, and focuses only on keyboard accessibility and UX enhancement.

title: Page renders before CSS/JS are fully loaded, causing flash during navigation
body:
When navigating between pages such as **Home**, **Tickets**, and **Talks**, the screen briefly flashes as if all JavaScript and CSS assets are being reloaded on every navigation. This results in a visible flicker where the UI momentarily resets before the target page is rendered.

The behavior is especially noticeable during frequent navigation and negatively impacts perceived performance and user experience.

**Expected behavior**  
Page-to-page navigation should feel smooth and seamless, without visible flashes or full reloading of styles and scripts. Ideally, shared CSS and JavaScript assets should persist across navigations, or transitions should be handled gracefully to avoid abrupt visual resets.

**Screenshots**  

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2b922cc3-d6a5-4b69-98fb-6e30e4c413ec

**Additional context**  

This issue appears to be related to the timing of route transitions versus asset readiness. A potential solution would be to delay rendering or route completion until the target page’s assets have been fully fetched and initialized, ensuring a clean handoff between pages.

This approach would address the root cause rather than masking the issue with a loader, while still allowing a minimal transition or loading state if needed. Investigation into routing hooks, asset preloading, and render lifecycle would help determine the most maintainable implementation.

title: Unify Event Navigation Buttons and Prevent Vertical Shifting
body:
# Unify Event Navigation Buttons and Prevent Vertical Shifting

## Describe the bug
The event navigation buttons (**Home, Tickets, Talk, Videos**) exhibit inconsistent positioning and styling across the application. When navigating between different event sections, specifically switching from **Home/Tickets** to the **Talk** dashboard, the entire navigation header shifts vertically.

This creates a visible layout jump that breaks visual continuity and negatively impacts user experience.

### Root causes
1. **Inconsistent Container Structure**
   - **Home/Tickets** use a `<nav id="event-nav">` wrapper.
   - **Talk Dashboard** uses a `<div id="main-title">` structure.

2. **Divergent CSS Rules**
   - Different vertical margins and padding are applied in:
     - `app/eventyay/static/eventyay-common/scss/custom.scss`
     - `app/eventyay/static/orga/css/_layout.css`

3. **Template Fragmentation**
   - Each section uses its own version of `component_link.html` (`orga`, `eventyay_common`, `control`).
   - This results in hardcoded `active` states and duplicated layout logic.

---

## Expected behavior
- The navigation buttons should maintain **consistent vertical and horizontal alignment** across all event-related pages.
- The header layout (**Event Name / Date followed by Navigation**) should be:
  - Unified into a single reusable component
  - Visually stable with no vertical shifting
  - Aligned with consistent borders, spacing, and styling

---

## Screenshots

| Home / Tickets Layout | Talk Dashboard Layout (Shifted) |
| :---: | :---: |
| ![Home/Tickets Navbar Position](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/076a3831-0b8f-4b58-9bae-2a20f086f437) | ![Talk Navbar Position Shift](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b73bf0d-69aa-428e-a37a-31ef7a142e4b) |


---

## Additional context
- The **Talk** section’s navigation layout is visually disparate compared to **Home/Tickets**.
- CSS rules contributing to the issue:
  - `#main-title .navigation-button` includes `margin-left: auto;` in `_layout.css`.
  - `#event-nav .navigation .navigation-button` applies `margin-top: 10px` at large screen sizes in `custom.scss`, which is absent elsewhere.
- A **single unified `component_link.html`** or a shared header fragment is required to address this systematically and eliminate layout drift.

title: Navigation buttons redirect to test.eventyay.com instead of staying on current domain
body: # Navigation buttons redirect to test.eventyay.com instead of staying on current domain ## Description When clicking on navigation buttons (Home, Tickets, Talk) in the eventyay web application, users are intermittently redirected to `test.eventyay.com` instead of staying on the current domain. This creates a disruptive user experience and breaks the navigation flow. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Navigate to any event page on localhost (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/aer/tq3vak/`) 2. Click on any of the following navigation buttons: - **Talk** button (from tickets/control section) - **Home** button (from talk/orga section) - **Tickets** button (from talk/orga section) 3. Observe that sometimes the browser redirects to `https://test.eventyay.com` instead of staying on `localhost:8000` ## Expected Behavior Clicking navigation buttons should keep users on the current domain and navigate to the correct section within the same application instance. **Example:** - Starting page: `http://localhost:8000/control/event/tq3vak/` - Click "Talk" button - Expected result: `http://localhost:8000/orga/event/tq3vak/` - **NOT**: `https://test.eventyay.com/orga/event/tq3vak/` ## Actual Behavior Navigation buttons sometimes redirect to `test.eventyay.com` (or whatever domain is configured in `TALK_HOSTNAME` or `SITE_URL`), causing: - Loss of current session context - Confusion for users - Broken development workflow on localhost - Potential security concerns (unintended cross-domain navigation) ## Affected Components ### Navigation Buttons: - ✗ Talk button (in control and eventyay_common sections) - ✗ Home button (in talk/orga section) - ✗ Tickets button (in talk/orga section) - ✗ Dashboard navigation links - ✗ Settings navigation links ### Affected Files: - JavaScript popover menus (`popover.js` files) - Navigation component templates (`component_link.html` files) - Settings page templates - Dashboard widgets ## Root Cause The application uses **absolute URLs** for navigation that depend on configuration settings: 1. **`TALK_HOSTNAME`** setting (from `eventyay.cfg`): Points to talk component domain 2. **`SITE_URL`** setting: Points to base application URL 3. **urlman `.full` property**: Constructs absolute URLs using these settings When these settings point to different domains (common in development/staging), navigation creates cross-domain links. **Technical Details:** ```python # Example problematic code: event.talk_dashboard_url # Uses TALK_HOSTNAME event.tickets_urls.tickets_home_common.full # Uses SITE_URL # When TALK_HOSTNAME='https://test.eventyay.com' and SITE_URL='http://localhost:8000' # Navigation creates cross-domain redirects ``` ## Environment - **Development**: `localhost:8000` redirects to `test.eventyay.com` - **Configuration**: `eventyay.cfg` with different `url` and `talk_hostname` values - **Affected**: All deployment environments where `TALK_HOSTNAME` ≠ `SITE_URL` ## Proposed Solution Replace absolute URLs with Django's relative URL resolution system: 1. **Templates**: Use `{% url %}` tags instead of `.full` properties 2. **JavaScript**: Read hostname from Django context, don't hardcode 3. **Python views**: Use `reverse()` instead of absolute URL properties **Example Fix:** ```django Talk Talk ``` ## Additional Context This issue was discovered during local development but affects all environments where navigation between the tickets and talk components occurs. The fix ensures navigation always stays on the current domain regardless of configuration. **Related Configuration Files:** - `eventyay.cfg` - `eventyay.development.toml` - `eventyay.production.toml` ## Checklist - [x] Navigation buttons stay on current domain - [ ] Home button works correctly - [ ] Tickets button works correctly - [ ] Talk button works correctly - [ ] Popover menus navigate correctly - [ ] Settings page navigation works - [ ] Dashboard links work correctly - [ ] All environments tested (localhost, staging, production)

# Concurrent Refund Requests Can Exceed Payment Amount (Financial Loss)

## Describe the bug

When two refund requests are processed simultaneously for the same payment, both can pass validation and create refunds that together exceed the payment amount.

title: Bug: Voucher Redemption Race Condition
body: # Bug: Voucher Redemption Race Condition ## Describe the bug The voucher redemption system has a critical race condition that allows multiple concurrent requests to exceed the `max_usages` limit. When multiple users attempt to redeem the same voucher simultaneously, the validation check occurs **before** acquiring the database lock, creating a window where all concurrent requests can pass validation and successfully redeem the voucher beyond its intended limit. **In our testing, a voucher with `max_usages=3` was successfully redeemed 5 times (167% over limit).** ### Root Cause The bug is located in `app/eventyay/base/services/cart.py`: 1. **Lines 1002-1021 (`_get_voucher_availability`)**: Voucher availability validation happens **without any lock** 2. **Lines 1358-1368 (`_require_locking`)**: Database lock is acquired **after** validation has already completed ## Expected behavior A voucher with `max_usages=3` should only allow **exactly 3 redemptions**. The 4th and 5th concurrent requests should fail with an error message indicating the voucher has reached its maximum usage limit. ## Screenshots ### Screenshot 1: Vouchers Page - Over-redemption Visible ### Screenshot 2: Orders Page - Multiple Orders with Same Voucher

title: Bug: Cart Expiry Race Condition Allows Order Overselling
body:
# Cart checkout allows overselling when lock is skipped

## The Problem

Found a race condition in `eventyay/base/services/orders.py` (lines 1180-1188) that lets multiple people buy the last ticket simultaneously.

The code has a "performance optimization" that skips locking the event during checkout when:
- No voucher is used
- Cart isn't expiring soon (>2 minutes left)
- No seat selection
```python
if positions.filter(
    Q(voucher__isnull=False) | Q(expires__lt=now() + timedelta(minutes=2)) | Q(seat__isnull=False)
).exists():
    # Performance optimization comment...
    locked = True
    lockfn = event.lock

with lockfn() as now_dt:
    # order creation
```

When that condition is false, `lockfn` stays as a no-op function and multiple checkouts can happen at once.

## What Happens

**Expected:** If there's 1 ticket left and 2 people checkout, only 1 should succeed.

**Actual:** Both succeed. You get 2 orders for a quota of 1.

## How to Reproduce

1. Create an event with 1 ticket available
2. Open two browser windows
3. Add the product to cart in both (make sure cart expires >2 mins away, no vouchers)
4. Click checkout in both windows at the same time
5. Both orders go through → quota shows 2/1 sold

Works consistently in testing, confirmed on test event `aer/xgzvvq` on local device 


## Related

Found this while fixing #1344 (payment duplicate confirmation bug). Same pattern.

body:
# Payment Duplicate Confirmation Returns Success

## Summary
Duplicate payment confirmation requests return HTTP 200/302 (success) instead of HTTP 409 (Conflict) or 422 (Unprocessable Entity). This breaks idempotency and prevents proper error handling in automated systems.

## Location
File: `/app/eventyay/base/models/orders.py`
Method: `OrderPayment.confirm()`
Lines: 1668-1677

## Current Behavior
```python
def confirm(self, ...):
    with transaction.atomic():
        locked_instance = OrderPayment.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=self.pk)
        if locked_instance.state == self.PAYMENT_STATE_CONFIRMED:
            logger.info('Confirmed payment {} but ignored due to likely race condition.'.format(self.full_id))
            return  # Returns None - appears as success to caller
```

When a payment is already confirmed:
- Method returns `None` silently
- HTTP response: 200 OK or 302 Found (success)
- Log message: "race condition" written but no exception raised
- Client cannot distinguish success from duplicate

## Expected Behavior
```python
def confirm(self, ...):
    with transaction.atomic():
        locked_instance = OrderPayment.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=self.pk)
        if locked_instance.state == self.PAYMENT_STATE_CONFIRMED:
            raise PaymentAlreadyConfirmedException(
                f'Payment {self.full_id} has already been confirmed.'
            )
```

Should return:
- HTTP 409 Conflict or 422 Unprocessable Entity
- Error response body with clear message
- Exception that can be caught and handled

## Reproduction Steps
1. Navigate to order with pending payment: `http://localhost:8000/control/event/aer/xgzvvq/orders/90DEK/`
2. Click "Mark as paid" - payment confirmed successfully
3. Open browser console and run:
```javascript
fetch('/control/event/aer/xgzvvq/orders/90DEK/payments/3/confirm', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {'X-CSRFToken': document.querySelector('[name=csrfmiddlewaretoken]').value},
    credentials: 'include'
}).then(r => console.log('Status:', r.status))
```
4. Observe: Returns 200 OK instead of 409 Conflict

## Evidence
Console output:
```
Status: 200 - Expected: 409, Actual: BUG
```

Server logs:
```
INFO 2025-11-24 17:05:20,410 runserver: HTTP POST /control/event/aer/xgzvvq/orders/90DEK/payments/3/confirm 302
INFO 2025-11-24 17:05:49,745 runserver: HTTP POST /control/event/aer/xgzvvq/orders/90DEK/payments/3/confirm 302
```

Both requests return 302 (success redirect). No error returned to client.

## Impact: Critical Use Cases

### 1. Payment Gateway Webhooks
**Scenario:** Stripe/PayPal sends duplicate webhook due to network retry or timeout.

```python
@webhook_handler('/stripe/webhook')
def process_stripe_webhook(payload):
    payment_id = payload['payment_intent']
    payment = OrderPayment.objects.get(provider_id=payment_id)
    
    result = payment.confirm()  # Returns None for both first and duplicate
    
    if result is None:  # TRUE for both requests!
        send_ticket_email(payment.order)  # Sent twice
        credit_user_account(payment.order.user, payment.amount)  # Credited twice
        trigger_fulfillment(payment.order)  # Processed twice
```

**Impact:** Duplicate tickets sent, double account credits, duplicate order processing.

### 2. API Client Retry Logic
**Scenario:** Mobile app or external integration implements retry on network failure.

```javascript
async function confirmPayment(paymentId) {
    try {
        const response = await api.post(`/payments/${paymentId}/confirm`);
        if (response.ok) {
            return {success: true};
        }
    } catch (error) {
        // Network timeout - retry
        const retry = await api.post(`/payments/${paymentId}/confirm`);
        if (retry.ok) {  // Also returns 200!
            return {success: true};  // Can't detect duplicate
        }
    }
}
```

**Impact:** Cannot implement safe retry logic. Cannot distinguish network failure from duplicate.

### 3. Background Job Idempotency
**Scenario:** Scheduled task processes pending payments, runs twice due to deployment or system error.

```python
# Cron job: Process bank transfers
def process_bank_transfers():
    for payment in get_received_bank_transfers():
        result = payment.confirm()
        # result is None for both first run and duplicate run
        metrics.increment('payments.confirmed')  # Counted twice
        send_notification(payment.order.user)  # Sent twice
```

**Impact:** Incorrect metrics, duplicate notifications, impossible to detect job ran twice.

### 4. Concurrent Admin Actions
**Scenario:** Two administrators or admin + automated system confirm same payment simultaneously.

```
Time 10:00:00.500 - Admin A clicks "Confirm payment"
Time 10:00:00.502 - Admin B clicks "Confirm payment"
Both receive 200 OK response
Neither knows the other just confirmed it
Audit logs show both succeeded
```

**Impact:** Confusion in audit logs, no clear indication of duplicate action, compliance issues.

### 5. Load Balancer Request Duplication
**Scenario:** Load balancer retries request on backend timeout.

```
Client -> Load Balancer -> Backend Server A (processing, slow response)
Load Balancer timeout (30s) -> Retry to Backend Server B
Both servers process the request
Both return 200 OK
```

**Impact:** Silent duplicate processing at infrastructure level, impossible to detect or prevent.

## Why This Matters

### Broken Idempotency Contract
REST APIs should be idempotent: same request multiple times = same result with clear indication.

**Current broken contract:**
- First request: 200 OK, payment confirmed
- Second request: 200 OK, payment already confirmed (but looks identical)
- Client cannot distinguish the two

**Correct idempotent contract:**
- First request: 200 OK, payment confirmed
- Second request: 409 Conflict, already confirmed (clearly different)
- Client can handle each appropriately

### No Error Signaling
Systems depend on HTTP status codes for automated decision-making:
- 2xx = Success, proceed
- 4xx = Client error, don't retry
- 5xx = Server error, retry later

Current behavior breaks this by returning 2xx for a client error (duplicate confirmation).

### Monitoring Blindness
Monitoring systems cannot detect issues:
- No errors logged at ERROR level
- No metrics for duplicate confirmations
- No alerts triggered
- Silent failures in production

### Data Integrity Risk
Without proper error handling:
- Financial reconciliation issues (duplicate credits)
- Inventory management issues (quota counting errors)
- Customer support issues (duplicate tickets/emails)
- Compliance issues (audit log ambiguity)

title: Export Functionality Broken
body:
# Export Functionality: Multiple Exporters Failing

## Problem Description

Following the fix for issue #1250 (HTTP 500 error preventing export page from loading), systematic testing reveals that approximately 7 out of 19 export options fail with "An unexpected error has occurred, please try again later" when attempting to generate exports.

The fix in PR #1258 successfully resolved the page load issue and form validation problems, but underlying issues within individual exporter implementations remain.

## Current Status

### Working Exporters (12 confirmed)
- All invoices
- Answers to file upload questions
- Check-in log (all successful scans)
- Email addresses (text file)
- Gift card redemptions
- Invoice data
- List of orders with taxes
- List of orders with taxes (PDF)
- Order overview (PDF)
- Order payments and refunds
- Quota availabilities
- Waiting list

### Failing Exporters (7 confirmed)
All display error message: "An unexpected error has occurred, please try again later"

- All PDF tickets in one file
- Attendee badges
- Check-in list
- Check-in list (PDF)
- Order data
- Order data (JSON)
- dekodi NREI (JSON)

## Technical Details

### Error Symptoms
- Export page loads successfully
- Forms render correctly
- Submission returns generic error message
- No specific error details shown to user
- HTTP 200 status returned (not 500)

### Observed Log Patterns
Docker logs show lxml.etree errors for some exporters:
```
lxml.etree.LxmlSyntaxError: inconsistent exit action in context manager
lxml.etree.LxmlSyntaxError: not in an element
```

These errors appear related to Excel/XML generation in openpyxl library interactions.


## Previously Fixed Issues

### Issue 1: Event.items vs Event.products
- **File**: `app/eventyay/plugins/checkinlists/exporters.py`
- **Problem**: Referenced non-existent Event.items relation
- **Solution**: Changed to Event.products
- **Status**: Fixed in PR #1258

### Issue 2: Missing JSON_FIELD_AVAILABLE Setting
- **Problem**: Setting undefined in settings.py
- **Solution**: Added based on database backend detection
- **Status**: Fixed in PR #1258

### Issue 3: Form Validation Logic
- **Files**: `control/views/orders.py`, `control/views/organizer.py`
- **Problem**: Unsafe cleaned_data access
- **Solution**: Safe access using getattr()
- **Status**: Fixed in PR #1258

## Testing Methodology

Testing performed at `/control/event/{organizer}/{event}/orders/export/`

For each exporter:
1. Navigate to export page
2. Select exporter from list
3. Fill required fields (if any)
4. Click generate/export button
5. Document success or failure with error message


## Related Work

- Original issue: #1250 - Unable to Export Order Data – HTTP 500 Error
- Fix PR: #1258 - Fixed page load and form validation
- Related models: Event, Product, Order, OrderPosition

title: Navigation Button Border Radius Inconsistency Between Tickets and Talk Components
body: **Describe the bug** The navigation buttons (Home, Tickets, Talk, Videos) display inconsistent border styling across different components of the EventYay platform. When viewing the Tickets component, the navigation buttons have sharp, rectangular corners, but when switching to the Talk component, the same navigation buttons display with rounded corners. This creates a jarring visual inconsistency that affects the overall user experience and design coherence. **Expected behavior** Navigation buttons should maintain consistent styling across all components of the platform. All navigation buttons (Home, Tickets, Talk, Videos) should have the same border-radius properties regardless of which component/section the user is currently viewing, ensuring a unified and professional appearance throughout the application. **Steps to Reproduce** Navigate to the Tickets section (/control/event/{event-name}/) Observe the navigation buttons in the header - they display with sharp, rectangular corners Click on the "Talk" button to switch to the Talk component (/orga/event/{event-name}/) Observe the same navigation buttons now display with rounded corners Compare the visual difference between the two states **Screenshots** **Additional context** This inconsistency occurs because different components (Tickets vs Talk) load different CSS files that apply conflicting styles to the navigation buttons. The issue affects: Visual consistency across the platform User experience and design professionalism Brand coherence Technical Details: Tickets Component: Uses CSS that renders buttons with border-radius: 0 or no border-radius Talk Component: Uses CSS that applies border-radius to create rounded corners Components affected: All header navigation buttons (Home, Tickets, Talk, Videos) Scope: Cross-component styling inconsistency
